contents:
The other day our group went on a circuit of the poorly guarded villages near Zasekov. These lands are important for husbandry, yet few hunters are sent there, since all the vampires were purged from those parts long ago, and the region is held to be quiet, for it lies far too distant from the borders. The last few years have been especially fruitful: bread has grown cheaper, so there seemed to be nothing to worry about. At present the country's hot spots have cooled off, so we were redirected to guard villages from which hunters had earlier been withdrawn, there being too few hands at the fortifications. Now it was decided to partly resume the patrols. Needless to say, the last thing we expected to find upon arrival was a graveyard without end. Not a sound was to be heard. All the people and animals seemed to have vanished, and a thick fog drifted down the streets. Some of the villagers we found already dead, but there was one girl, in her teens, who turned out to be alive. Part of her leg was missing, as though it had been bitten off, and she looked starved, as did all the bodies we had found. At first, she, too, seemed dead, but unlike the others she was still breathing. We halted for a short while so that the healers might give her first aid.

When the girl came to, she told us that the village had died of hunger: this year something had befallen the crops, and the squire had seized whatever stores were left, along with the livestock. No one was let into the town, and the villagers were forbidden to enter the woods, since those belonged to the squire — and so the people began to starve.

When we asked about her leg, she said that ever since all this began, she had been seeing a certain “prymara” in the fog. By her telling, it resembled an old woman with a jutting jaw and bony hands, a cloak hiding her eyes and nose. Its body was twisted, and everything but the head and hands was shapeless. She likened its skin to a spider’s, though we ourselves are not quite sure what she meant by it. The more people died, and the more certain death by starvation became, the closer this foul creature dared to approach, reaching out its rotten, crumbling limbs to the girl, beckoning, calling to her. When the old woman at last stood close beside her, she seized the girl by the leg and began to consume her, bit by bit. The girl lost consciousness.

Among the common folk there are indeed tales of such “prymaras”, yet for my part I incline to think she imagined it, given the plight she found herself in. Perhaps it was either another starving soul, but then one must ask what became of them afterwards, or, more likely, she did it to herself, there being no other way left. I will not go into the details. As we later saw for ourselves, the fields really were stricken with some sort of blight, but questions for the nobleman remain all the same, the more so as these lands are but a small part of his holdings. By evening I will draw up a report on this matter for my superiors.
